description_full: AbbVie Inc., a research-based biopharmaceutical company, engages in the research and development, manufacturing, commercializing, and sale of medicines and therapies worldwide. The company offers Skyrizi to treat autoimmune diseases; Rinvoq to treat inflammatory diseases; Imbruvica for the treatment of adult patients with blood cancers; Venclexta to treat blood cancers; Elahere to treat various cancer; and Epkinly to treat lymphoma; and Emrelis for the treatment of lung cancer. It also provides facial injectables, plastics and regenerative medicine, body contouring, and skincare products; botox Cosmetic for the treatment of glabellar lines, crow's feet, forehead lines, and platysma bands; Juvederm Collection to treat volume loss in the temples, undereye, cheeks, chin, lips and lower face; Vraylar to treat schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and depressive disorder; Duodopa to treat Parkinson's disease; Ubrelvy to treat migraine; Qulipta for episodic and chronic migraine; and Vyalev for the treatment of motor fluctuations, as well as Botox Therapeutic to treat chronic migraine, overactive bladder, spasticity, cervical dystonia, and other conditions. In addition, the company offers Ozurdex for visual impairment; Lumigan/Ganfort and Alphagan/Combigan for the reduction of elevated intraocular pressure in patients with open angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension; and other eye care products, including Refresh/Optive, Xen, Durysta, and Restasis. Further, it provides Mavyret to treat chronic hepatitis C virus genotype 1-6 infection; Creon, a pancreatic enzyme therapy; and Linzess/Constella to treat irritable bowel syndrome with constipation and chronic idiopathic constipation. The company was incorporated in 2012 and is headquartered in North Chicago, Illinois.

financial_summary: AbbVie Inc. is a mega-cap healthcare business with a $514.9B market cap on $61.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +10% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 17% against a 8% cost of capital, a 9-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $17.8B in free cash flow — roughly 29 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 4.50× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -11.1% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.5× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 5.2×.

Shareholder yield of 2.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 25% over the past year excluding the latest month.

val: The stock trades 20% below its DCF fair value of $362, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 28%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $197 to $676 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Healthcare peers: P/E 50.1 vs 25.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 150% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.6% (vs the 8% bar).

prof: ROIC of 17% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.49).
It converts 29% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 4.50x, but high accruals (-11.1% of assets).
It spends 14.9% of revenue on R&D and 1.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.5x net debt to EBITDA ($5.3B of cash against $61.4B of debt), with interest covered 5.2x.
The current ratio of 0.67 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.8% over 3 years, 6.0% over 5 years and 10.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 1.2% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 1.6x depreciation (2.0% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 34, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 77%.
It returns 2.5% a year to shareholders (0.2% in buybacks and 2.4% in dividends).
It pays out 117% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 57,000 employees, each generates about $1.1M of revenue, 2.8x the Healthcare median, and productivity has risen 10.3% a year.
That works out to $313K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $7.4M (7x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
